intuition: Keep possible maximum positions in a queue whose values decrease from front to back. A newer value can replace older candidates that are no larger, because it will remain in the window longer. Remove positions that have left the window. The front then gives the maximum.

Store only values that can still become a future window maximum, using their indices for expiration. An older value no larger than a newly arrived value is permanently dominated: the new value is at least as useful and survives longer. Removing such values from the deque’s back leaves decreasing candidates.

The oldest remaining candidate sits at the front, where expiry and maximum lookup are both immediate. The deque is not the complete window; discarded values remain in the input but are no longer relevant to this question.

The deque contains current-window candidates in decreasing value order. Any removed back candidate has a newer value no smaller, so it cannot become the maximum before it expires. Expired front indices are invalid. Thus the front is the largest value among all relevant candidates and the true maximum. Each index enters once and leaves at most once from either end.

steps: After reading 1 and 3, remove index 0 because newer value 3 dominates 1.
Read -1 to complete the first window; candidates [1,2] give maximum 3.
Read -3; index 1 is still present, so the next maximum remains 3.
Read 5: expire index 1, then remove the smaller back candidates; maximum becomes 5.

concept.question: Why can a newer larger value erase an older smaller maximum candidate?
intuition: Scanning every window repeats maximum comparisons. Not every current value deserves to remain a future candidate.

Keep candidate positions in a queue with decreasing values. A newer value at least as large as an older candidate dominates it: it is better now and will expire later. Remove expired front positions, and read the maximum from the remaining front.
concept.observation: An older candidate no larger than a newer one can be removed permanently.
approach: Remove candidates that have left the current window.
Remove weaker candidates from the back before adding the new position.
Read the front candidate once the window is complete.
concept.correctness: Every removed weaker candidate has a newer replacement at least as large, so it cannot become maximum before that replacement expires. Expired candidates cannot influence the current window. The decreasing queue therefore retains a valid dominating representative for every discarded active value, and its front is the window maximum.

complexity.explanation: Each position enters once and leaves at most once from either end. Work is linear; candidate memory is bounded by the window width, plus output.

scenes.title: Three dominates one
scenes.narration: For width 3, values 1 then 3 arrive. The newer 3 removes 1 from candidacy. With -1, the first maximum is 3.
scenes.decision: The newer larger value also remains available longer.

scenes.title: Five replaces the weaker candidates
scenes.narration: The next maximum is still 3. When 5 arrives, the old 3 expires and the smaller remaining candidates are removed.
scenes.decision: Candidate removal does not alter the actual input window.

scenes.title: Later windows expose later maxima
scenes.narration: The remaining windows have maxima 5,6,7. Return [3,3,5,5,6,7].
scenes.decision: Each front is the greatest unexpired undominated value.

scenes.narration: Every removed weaker candidate has a newer replacement at least as large, so it cannot become maximum before that replacement expires. Expired candidates cannot influence the current window. The decreasing queue therefore retains a valid dominating representative for every discarded active value, and its front is the window maximum.

scenes.title: A boundary to remember
scenes.narration: Equal values at different positions can replace older equal candidates; keep the newer one because it expires later.
scenes.decision: Store positions so expiration can be tested.
